_comment: Baselines for scripts/screenshot.sh. Numbers here are measurements from a real run, not hand-picked targets. Regenerate with `scripts/screenshot.sh --update` after a deliberate visual change, then read the printed diff before committing — a diff that isn't explained by your change means something regressed. The app is run against a throwaway seeded library, so every number below is a measurement of src/seed.rs rendered by this repository and of nothing else; it used to be read out of whoever's real library happened to be on the machine, which made the net go red for reasons no diff could show. Keep this file formatted exactly as `jq .` emits it: --update rewrites it through jq, so matching jq's formatting is what keeps an --update diff down to the numbers that actually changed.

logical_window.note: The logical (CSS-pixel) window the app asks for — WIDTH/HEIGHT in src/lib.rs. Every region below is written in these CSS pixels, the same units the source code uses, so a human can check `right: 36` against the `right: 20px` in src/screens/library.rs without doing arithmetic. The capture is physical pixels, so the script converts by a scale factor it derives as captured_height / 852. Height, not width, and that choice is load-bearing: the window manager is free to ignore the size the app asks for, and this one does — it has granted 491x1065 and later 550x1065 for the very same request, i.e. it stretched the width and left the height alone. 1065 = 852 x 1.25 exactly on this 1.25x display, so the height is the dimension that still carries the scale factor honestly; the width no longer does and must never be used to derive it. If a window manager ever starts stretching the height too, this derivation breaks and the right fix is to ask the compositor for the scale factor, not to re-record the numbers below.

region_schema.note: Every region states the edge of the *captured image* it hangs off, because the window manager decides the capture size and absolute WxH+X+Y coordinates slide off their target the moment it changes its mind. `anchor` is required and must be one of the six below; the offsets are CSS pixels measured inward from the anchored edge to the nearest edge of the region, and `w`/`h` are its CSS-pixel size.

anchors.top: spans the capture width; requires `top` and `w`: "full"
anchors.bottom: spans the capture width; requires `bottom` and `w`: "full"

region_schema.self_test: `scripts/screenshot.sh --self-test` resolves every region below against five capture sizes and asserts the arithmetic, without building or launching anything.

checks.name: thumb_painted
checks.description: The library's first row 38x38 attachment thumb is actually painted, not just laid out. Caught the display:contents paint regression (docs/RINCH.md: 'The paint regression') where boxes were sized correctly but never drawn.
checks.note: Reference: ~0.907 painted (grey fill over paper), ~0.970 unpainted (bare paper) — a delta far outside tolerance. Top-left anchored because the content column starts at the left edge: this region measures byte-identically at 491x1065 and 550x1065, which is the proof that a left anchor is the right one for it.

checks.name: fab_solid_accent
checks.description: The library FAB (bottom-right, add song) is filled with the accent colour across its whole interior, so anything painting over it is caught.
checks.note: The FAB is `position: absolute; right: 20px; bottom: 16px; width: 60px; height: 60px` in src/screens/library.rs, so it hangs off the bottom-right corner and nothing else. Its `bottom: 16px` is measured from the Library screen box, which ends above the bottom nav, so this region's `bottom: 100` is that 16px plus the rendered height of the nav strip — a text metric, not a constant, and therefore measured rather than derived. The region is the FAB's interior with the 20px corner radius cleared on all four sides, and it deliberately INCLUDES the plus glyph rather than dodging it: the glyph is drawn in the on-accent colour and costs about 3% of the sampled pixels, which is why the threshold is 0.94 and not 0.97. That headroom is the check. Card K14 recorded a row's confidence dots painting on top of this button at a 491px window width and not at 550px — paint order varying with viewport width, which cannot happen now that joeleaver/rinch#292 derives paint order and hit-test order from one `(z_index, dom_order)` sequence with no viewport term in it. Until that PR landed this region sampled only the FAB's lower band, deliberately clear of the dots, which meant the net could not have caught the fault coming back. It samples the whole interior now: three dots cost roughly 4% of these pixels, enough to drop the match below the threshold. Checked by deleting the FAB's `z-index: 10` and rerunning this script: the measured fraction did not move, so the button now paints on top on its own and the workaround is no longer load-bearing for paint. What it still cannot promise is a dot landing outside this region — the overlapping row's position depends on scroll, so no fixed rectangle covers every case.

checks.name: confidence_dots_on_screen
checks.description: The first library row's three confidence dots are painted in the accent colour at the row's right edge, inside the captured window. This is card A2's own check: on a HiDPI display, these are the pixels that fell off the right edge of the page.
checks.note: Card A2: the desktop shell laid the document out at the window's physical surface size and then painted it scaled by that same factor again, so on this machine's 1.25x display a fifth of the page fell off the right edge of the window — and `ConfidenceDots` (src/ui.rs), the last flex child of every `SongRow`, sits at that exact edge. joeleaver/rinch#246 fixes it upstream by laying out at the logical size instead; `src/bin/probe.rs` demonstrates the fault in isolation and `cargo run --release --bin probe` rows A, B and D are the general-purpose regression, but nothing before this check exercised the real symptom through the real screen — a purple box in a 460x300 toy window is not the same claim as three specific pixels of the library screen the handoff actually promises a user. This is that check. It targets the first row (Landslide, seeded Solid) specifically because Solid is the one confidence level that paints all three dots at full accent rather than the dimmed tone Rusty and Learning use (`Confidence::dot_color`, src/model.rs) — the biggest, most reliable target this screen offers pixel-comparison. The region was not derived from the CSS the way thumb_painted's or the FAB's were; it was measured directly off a real 1.25x capture (`convert … txt:` sampled along both axes through the dot cluster) and only then converted back to the CSS pixels this file is written in, because the row's own right edge is the thing under test and computing it from the same layout constants the bug corrupts would have proven nothing. The measured ink ran from CSS x 344.8 to 371.2 (dead on 26 px: three 6px dots plus two 4px gaps, `gap: 4px` in `ConfidenceDots`) and y 286.4 to 292.8 (a 6.4px dot, against the 6px `ConfidenceDots` draws) — a right offset of 21.8 CSS from the window edge, which is `SCREEN_PAD` (22px, src/theme.rs) almost exactly, because the row list's own `padding: 0 SCREEN_PAD 90px` (src/screens/library.rs) is the only thing standing between the dots and the window edge. `right: 18, w: 34` and `top: 282, h: 16` wrap that measurement with three to five CSS pixels of margin on every side, the same generous-but-not-loose margin fab_solid_accent's note describes, so ordinary anti-aliasing jitter does not make this check as fragile as the thing it is meant to catch. Anchored top-right rather than top-left, unlike thumb_painted: the dots hang off the row's right edge, which tracks the window's right edge as the window manager's grant varies, not the content column's left edge, which does not move. Threshold: this run measured 117/860 pixels matching #B54724 at 20% fuzz in this exact region; min_matched is 85% of that (99), the same margin --update would have written for any other accent_presence check, computed by hand rather than through --update so that re-running --update for this one check would not also perturb every other check's threshold with this run's own jitter. If this check goes red while `probe`'s rows A, B and D still show their purple box, suspect this region or this screen specifically, not the rinch pin.

checks.name: group_header_accent
checks.description: The first library group header's label (e.g. 'SOLID') is painted in the accent colour, not the muted grey later headers use.

checks.name: group_header_double_paint
checks.description: The first library group header's label ('SOLID') is drawn once. Card K20: it was drawn twice, 'SOLID' with 'Solid' struck through it, and no colour check could see it.
checks.note: The net had a group-header check already — group_header_accent, which counts accent pixels — and it was green through the whole of the K20 fault, because a run painted twice in the accent colour is still the accent colour and there are simply more of them than the min_matched floor of 40 asks for. Every other check here samples colour and none of them could have caught it either; the fault was found on a phone, by eye, in a screenshot taken for a different card. This check is the one that would have. Why this header and not any other text: T_LABEL_CAPS (src/theme.rs) styles it 'text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 0.16em', and those two properties live in the IFC text builder and nowhere else. The correct copy is therefore 'SOLID', tracked; the duplicate the paint walk drew was the raw DOM string 'Solid', untracked and untransformed, at a different width and a different set of glyph shapes. Two copies that disagree that strongly leave far more ink in the same rectangle than one does — 0.1025 against the 0.0618 recorded here, a 66% difference against a 0.012 tolerance — which is what makes an ink_extent check the right instrument. Text with no transform and no tracking in a root with no padding double-paints exactly on top of itself and is invisible even to this, which is why the region is pointed here rather than at a song title. The trimmed ink box does not move between the two renders (38x9 either way): the duplicate starts at the same x and is narrower, so it adds density, not extent. Width and height are recorded anyway because they catch a different failure — the same region under the DejaVu fallback reads 0.7636 / 0.4000 / 0.0669, so this check happens to police the app's own typefaces here too, on all three axes. Top-left anchored: the group header sits in the content column at SCREEN_PAD, which starts at the left edge and does not move when the window manager grants a different width. The region stops at 44 CSS px wide so that the count ('5') to the right of the label, and the hairline after it, stay out of the crop — the label's ink ends around 37 CSS px in and the count begins around 48.

checks.name: bottom_nav_accent
checks.description: The bottom nav strip carries the accent colour: the active item (Songs, selected by default) has its icon and its label painted in it, and it is the only thing in the strip that is ever accent — the inactive item is muted grey and the hairline and the paper are neither.
checks.note: Spans the whole capture width on purpose. The two nav items are `flex: 1`, so the active one re-centres over the left half whenever the window manager grants a different width — there is no fixed x it can be sampled at. Counting accent pixels across the full strip is the same assertion, because nothing else in the strip is accent; what it gives up is the ability to say *which* item is active, which this check never asserted in a way pixels could tell apart anyway.

checks.name: screen_background
checks.description: The screen background is the light-mode paper colour, sampled from the empty status-bar strip at the very top.
checks.note: The safe-area strip the OS status bar sits in. It is empty across the full width at every window size, so the top-left corner of it is background under any grant the window manager can make.

checks.name: screen_title_glyph
checks.description: The library screen title ('Songs') is drawn in the app's own display face, not whatever serif the platform happened to have lying around. Card A4: every check above this one samples colour, and colour cannot tell Newsreader from DejaVu Serif — the accent, the paper and the fill are the same hex codes under either face. This one looks at the letters themselves.
checks.note: Region: top-left anchored (the content column starts at the left edge, same reasoning as thumb_painted) over the 'Songs' title — SCREEN_PAD (22px) in from the left, past the phone-standin status bar (44px) and most of the title block's own top padding (6px). Sized generously (160x42 CSS) so the crop holds the whole word with margin on every side and stops short of the meta line ('N in your book...') below it, which is a different, smaller face at a different weight and would muddy the measurement if it leaked in. Threshold 50%: ink is #1C1917 on #FBF7F0 paper in light mode, nowhere near each other in lightness, so the exact cut point does not matter. Card K20 moved every number here and is the reason they are what they are. Until that fix, every run of text in an inline formatting context was painted twice — once by its IFC root and once again by the standalone text path, which draws the raw string with none of the styling — so this region was measuring 'Songs' struck through with a second, differently-shaped 'Songs'. That is what the old 0.0863 ink fraction and 0.7736 height fraction were measurements of. The single copy this check now samples reads 0.4950 / 0.7547 / 0.0717. Worth knowing that this check is what caught the change: the five colour checks above it did not move by a pixel, because removing a duplicate paint of the same colour in the same place changes no hue anywhere. The tolerances were re-derived at the same time, because the fix narrowed the gap this check exists to see. Forcing the DejaVu Serif fallback (drop the serif and sans-serif entries from `crate::FONTS`, rebuild, capture) used to read 0.56 / 0.75 / 0.113 — but the 0.113 was mostly the double paint, whose two copies diverge much further in a face the app never chose. On a single-copy render DejaVu reads 0.4500 / 0.7547 / 0.0626, so the honest separations are 0.045 on width and 0.0091 on ink pixels, and the tolerances below (0.02 and 0.006) leave margins of 0.025 and 0.0031 respectively. Both axes still trip on the wrong face, which is the whole point; neither has room to spare, and a capture is byte-deterministic on this machine (two consecutive runs differ in 0 pixels), so tight is affordable here in a way it would not be against a noisy source. The height tolerance stays deliberately loose at 0.08: these two faces share a cap-height at this size — post-fix they measure the *same* 0.7547 — so that axis discriminates nothing between them and is only guarding against a blank title or a wholesale typographic change.

checks.name: background_has_no_accent
checks.description: NEGATIVE CONTROL. The opposite corner of that same empty status-bar strip contains no accent pixels at all. Nothing about the app can make this fail; only the checking machinery can.
checks.note: Every other check here is of the form 'this colour is present', and a suite made only of those passes just as happily when the colour comparison has quietly started matching everything — a stuck `compare`, an ImageMagick whose -fuzz argument changed meaning, a crop that silently resolves to the whole image. This one asserts the negative through the exact same sampling path, at the same 20% fuzz the accent-presence checks use, over a region that is guaranteed paper. If it ever goes red, do not look at the app: look at this script and at ImageMagick. It is also why --update refuses to re-record it — a control whose threshold is measured from the run it is meant to be policing is not a control.
